questions.q: In the lab's three-unit pipeline split (normalize / submit_and_wait / aggregate), which unit(s) can be unit-tested with hardcoded inputs and zero QPU cost?
options: normalize and aggregate, since both are pure functions with no network dependency
Only normalize; aggregate always requires live measurement counts
None of them; all three require a real circuit execution to test
Only submit_and_wait, since it's the most important function
questions.explain: normalize and aggregate are pure functions -- no I/O, no network call -- so they can be tested instantly with hardcoded inputs. Only submit_and_wait touches the network/QPU and needs an integration test.

questions.q: The lab's normalization test feeds [2,2,2,2] into normalize(). What is the correct expected output, and why?
options: [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5], because the norm is sqrt(4x4)=4 and each entry 2/4=0.5, with squared entries summing to 1.0
[2, 2, 2, 2], unchanged, because normalization doesn't affect equal-valued vectors
[0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25], because each entry is divided by 8
[1, 1, 1, 1], because normalization always produces all-ones vectors
questions.explain: Sum of squares = 4x(2^2) = 16, norm = sqrt(16) = 4, so each entry becomes 2/4 = 0.5. The resulting vector's squared entries sum to 4x(0.5^2) = 1.0, confirming correct normalization.

questions.q: The lab's sign-convention test feeds aggregate() the synthetic counts {"0": 1000, "1": 0}. What must the correct output be, and what does this test catch?
options: There is no correct expected value for this synthetic input
Exactly -1.0, since |0> always maps to a negative eigenvalue
Exactly 0.5, since half the possible outcomes are being counted
Exactly +1.0; it catches a sign-convention bug that would flip this to -1.0 or some other wrong value, without needing ambiguous real-world data
questions.explain: With every one of 1,000 shots measuring |0>, the correct expectation value under the standard convention (|0>->+1) is exactly +1.0. A sign-flip bug would produce -1.0 instead, which this known-answer test catches immediately.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that testing pre/post-processing against synthetic, known-answer inputs matters MORE in hybrid quantum pipelines than in typical classical pipelines?
options: Quantum pipelines never produce plausible-looking wrong answers, so bugs are always obvious
A sign-flip or normalization bug produces a plausible-looking but incorrect number with no crash, and real quantum problems often have no independent ground truth to sanity-check against
Classical pipelines don't need any testing at all, unlike quantum ones
Synthetic test data is only useful for quantum pipelines, never for classical ones
questions.explain: Unlike typical classical bugs that often produce obviously-wrong output, a sign-flip or bad normalization in a hybrid pipeline yields a plausible number -- and because real quantum results often have no independent ground truth, known-answer synthetic tests are the only reliable way to catch these bugs.

questions.q: Why is splitting a pipeline into normalize / submit_and_wait / aggregate preferable to one long run_pipeline(raw_data) function, according to the lab?
options: It makes the code run faster on the QPU itself
It eliminates the need for any unit testing at all
It isolates the only network-dependent step, letting the pure pre/post-processing logic be tested independently and cheaply instead of requiring a real circuit run to exercise any part of the logic
It is required by every quantum cloud provider's SDK
questions.explain: A single monolithic function forces every test to also exercise the network/QPU call. Splitting the pipeline isolates that one dependency so the pure classical logic around it can be tested fast and cheaply, independent of hardware availability or cost.
